title: Disclosure notice, explicit saved facts, then a constrained shortlist
notice: Synthetic and illustrative. Card names, facts and identifiers are invented. Arguments follow the server's input schemas; results show only some of the fields the server returns.
demonstrates: The assistant explains what is saved, including request history, before the first Rewardopedia call.
Only explicit statements are saved, as structured entries with a new requestId.
recommend_cards reads saved context itself; it does not save anything.
A clearly named goal is mapped to its goal token, and the assistant says which goal it used.
A card whose fee is unknown does not pass a fee constraint, and a cap without a known amount is described as a cap of unknown size.

steps.text: I already have the Example Cash Card. Dining is my priority and I don't want an annual fee over $95.

Before I use Rewardopedia: it keeps a sanitized history of each Rewardopedia request in your Rewardopedia account until you delete it, and it saves facts you tell me, such as the cards you hold and your goals and constraints, unless you ask me not to. Both are shared across assistants connected to your account, and you can ask what is saved or ask me to forget it at any time. Please don't share card or account numbers. Shall I save that you hold the Example Cash Card, that your goal is dining, and that your annual fee limit is $95?

I used your dining goal and your $95 annual fee limit, and left out the Example Cash Card because you already have it. One card fits: the Example Dining Card. It earns 3 Example Points per $1 on dining, but that rate has an annual cap and Rewardopedia doesn't have the cap amount, so check the issuer's terms before relying on it. Its annual fee is $95 and it has no foreign transaction fee. Example Points are not cash, so their value depends on how you redeem them. One other card was left out because its annual fee is unknown, so it can't be shown to meet your limit.
